item.title: Xuxo Lore
item.description: The culinary logic of the xuxo - fry the dough, stuff it with something sweet and dairy-based, coat the outside in sugar - is so deeply embedded in Southern food tradition that attributing its invention to a Catalan acrobat requires a certain willful incuriosity about where good fried things actually come from.
item.content:encoded:
There are two official theories about where the xuxo comes from. The first involves an acrobat, a sneeze, and a pastry chef’s daughter in Girona, Catalonia, sometime in the 1920s. The second suggests the name derives from the French choux, the light dough used in profiteroles and éclairs. The xuxo isn’t made with choux dough, so that one doesn’t really hold up. And the acrobat one? We’ll flip that one a few times as unrealistic. The Catalan government has designated the xuxo a Producte de la Terra, a traditional regional product, which is a serious designation for a pastry whose origin story hinges on a man sneezing in a bakery.

There is a third theory.

We know that the xuxo is fried dough filled with a custard cream and rolled in sugar. In Catalonia, this is considered a regional delicacy with a romantic origin. In Alabama, this is called Tuesday. The culinary logic of the xuxo - fry the dough, stuff it with something sweet and dairy-based, coat the outside in sugar - is so deeply embedded in Southern food tradition that attributing its invention to a Catalan acrobat requires a certain willful incuriosity about where good fried things actually come from.

The American Gulf Coast has been producing fried custard-stuffed pastries for generations. Beignets, fried pies, custard fritters: the tradition is long, varied, and specifically concentrated in the region running from Mobile, Alabama across to East Texas. The crema catalana that fills a xuxo is, in spirit and in substance, a vanilla custard with a Spanish accent. It is not far from what comes out of a Southern kitchen on any given afternoon. The laminated dough is a refinement. The sugar coating is instinct.

Mobile, Alabama lives on the Gulf Coast. And it’s got history. It was founded French in 1702, passed into Spanish control in 1780, and held by Spain for nearly four decades before becoming American territory. That’s a pretty huge Spanish connection. Additionally, the oldest Mardi Gras celebration in America is in Mobile (definitely not New Orleans, Mobilians are sensitive about this), and its roots run directly back to French and Spanish colonial culture. The Gulf Coast and the Iberian peninsula have been in conversation, culturally and commercially, for three centuries.

By the early 1920s — the period in which the xuxo supposedly appears, fully formed, in Girona, with no named baker and no credited bakery — Gulf Coast food was moving widely - worldwide-ly. Pecans were being traded internationally. The port of Mobile was active. People traveled. Recipes traveled with them.

So, the third theory: sometime in the early 1920s, someone from the Gulf Coast was in Girona. A merchant. A traveler. Whoever. Someone whose grandmother fried things and whose instinct, in any kitchen in any country, was to fry something, fill it with custard, and roll it in sugar. This person snuck into a bakery one night to make something to remind them of home. Something they’d watched their grandmother cook hundreds of times. They baked that old magic, the Mobilian proto-xuxo (or “good ol’ fried-up flaky biscuits with warm pudding in them” - well, it wasn’t really named, as such, it was described). To account for breaking in they left a dozen filled xuxos in a bread basket on the kitchen counter. The Catalan Twelve, the first twelve residents who’d had one of the Mobilian originals,immediately recognized it as excellent, which it was, because it came from a place that had been perfecting this logic for generations. They claimed it as their own, though, when they wrote it down. They named it after a sneeze because they needed a story and the acrobat was handy.

Consider the evidence.

The real story is Alabama.

I cannot totally prove this and I acknowledge that. The Catalan Twelve likely have a lot to do with that. But consider what you’re being asked to believe instead, that a Catalan acrobat, caught in a bakery with a pastry chef’s daughter, spontaneously invented a fried laminated custard pastry as a peace offering, named it after the sound of his own sneeze, and that this pastry then became so beloved that the Catalan government formally designated it a traditional regional product a century later.

I’m not saying that didn’t happen. It’s not provable, either; nor is it quite believable. What I am saying is that Mobile was right there, and this theory holds water.

The xuxo is excellent. But whatever its origins, the Gulf Coast would claim it without hesitation, and the Gulf Coast has good taste. That much, at least, is not a theory.

item.title: 15 Minutes to Xuxos
item.description: Qué Sweet is the pastry and ice cream counter inside Mercado Little Spain; The signature item is the xuxo (pronounced roughly SHOO-sho), a pastry from Girona, in Catalonia.
item.content:encoded:
Another week, another bakery. And this one is just a 15-minute round trip walk from the office.

Qué Sweet is the pastry and ice cream counter inside Mercado Little Spain, José Andrés' 35,000-square-foot Spanish food hall at Hudson Yards, a collaboration with Ferran and Albert Adrià designed to recreate the logic of a Spanish mercado in Manhattan.

The signature item is the xuxo (pronounced roughly SHOO-sho), a pastry from Girona, in Catalonia, dating to the 1920s. The origin story involves an acrobat, a pastry chef's daughter, a well-timed sneeze, and an exchange of recipes in lieu of getting thrown out of the bakery. Whether or not that's true, the Catalan government has formally recognized the xuxo as a Producte de la Terra, a designation for traditional regional products.

Structurally, it's laminated dough filled with crema catalana-style pastry cream, deep fried, and rolled in sugar. What you get is a small golden cylinder, lightly sugared and slightly blistered from frying, that manages to feel improbably light. The exterior gives a faint crackle. Inside: soft, elastic fried dough and cold pastry cream. It's somewhere between a filled doughnut and a fried croissant, executed with excellent judgment.

Beyond the xuxo, the counter offers crema catalana, Basque-style cheesecake, and soft serve built around Spanish flavor traditions. Desserts that feel intentionally regional rather than trend-chasing. And if you're coming back and really want to go next level, there's the xuxo helado — the same pastry split or filled with soft serve, then finished with sauces or toppings.

What an awesome thing to get out of a 15-minute break. I got three xuxos just in case I felt like I wanted to share and/or give myself an xo later (by way of xuxo, if you will).

item.title: Step Challenge = Smør & Dominique Ansel
item.description: I fortunately stumbled upon a couple of bakeries during my work step challenge: Smør & Dominique Ansel.
item.content:encoded:
I recently visited Smør in Williamsburg, Brooklyn — a Scandinavian bakery with cardamom buns and all kinds of amazing things. This is their second location; the original, in the East Village, was started in 2019 by two Danes. I've lived in my neighborhood for a long time, and I had no idea this location existed until I stumbled upon it on a walk around my neighborhood during a step challenge at work. I remember when the bakery used to be occupied by an HVAC company with a large garage door — I always wondered why they needed it. Air conditioners aren't that tall.

Smør has made good use of the 3,000-square-foot space, and that old garage door opening can be opened up during nice weather. It functions as both an R&D lab and a counter-service bakery, and the kitchen is open-concept — you can see the workers making the pastries. Their mixers are enormous (see image below). They've got fresh sourdough, rye bread, pastries, sandwiches, and rotating loaves including dark chocolate-cherry, olive, seeded, and heritage grain varieties like Einkorn and Danko rye, plus Danish pastries like Hindbærsnitter (raspberry shortbread) and Drømmekage ("Dream Cake"). I got a cardamom bun, a cinnamon bun, and a fantastic Scandinavian donut and felt like I'd really accomplished something.

I hope you've heard of the Cronut, created at Dominique Ansel Bakery in SoHo. As it happened, still doing a work step challenge, I walked past it, thought "that's cool, never been there," and kept going. Then I realized: What am I doing? I'm never in SoHo. So, I turned around and walked on in. While it's most famous as the birthplace of the Cronut — Ansel's half-donut, half-croissant creation filled with ganaches and jams, with a new flavor each month — it's also the birthplace of the DKA (Dominique's Kouign Amann), the Cookie Shot, Frozen S'mores, and Blossoming Hot Chocolate. I picked up the cronut of the month — strawberries and cream brown butter — plus a pistachio crème-filled, pistachio-encrusted piece of heaven. The cronut lived up to the hype.

I'd attempted to visit Radio Bakery in Greenpoint this past Sunday, but I was thwarted by the Five Boro Bike Tour — Greenpoint was cut in half and I couldn't get past the blockades. It'll happen.

item.title: 15-Minutes to Li-Lac and Back
item.description: A hundred-year-old chocolate shop, less than ten minutes from my desk, making things by hand. What is right in the world? This.
item.content:encoded:
One of the perks of working where I work in the city is being so close to great food. But we don't know the half of what's out there. I don't anyway. Sometimes the best thing you can do on an afternoon break is explore. Take 15 mins. That's all you need, and you need it.

A co-worker recently challenged me to go on a little field trip during a 15-minute afternoon break: walk a loop from our office over to Li-Lac Chocolates at The Shops in Hudson Yards and back. It would count as a walk, a break, a little neighborhood education, and — crucially — by taking the field trip, I could experience real chocolate.

Li-Lac Chocolates is Manhattan's oldest chocolate house and has been making chocolate in New York City since 1923, when a Greek immigrant named George Demetrious opened a shop on Christopher Street in Greenwich Village. His original recipes — almond bark, hazelnut truffle squares, fudge — are still the ones in use today, made in small batches by hand. The company changed ownership a few times over the decades and now has six locations across the city, including a Hudson Yards shop near my office. It's a small chocolatier that never automated, never reinvented itself, and is still around over a century later because of that.

A hundred-year-old chocolate shop, less than ten minutes from my desk, making things by hand. What is right in the world? This.

And so of course I went. I timed it at 22 minutes for the entire loop — but I didn't know where the elevators were in the Shops at Hudson Yards, and then it took some time to merely ponder the chocolate, much less choose what to buy. Wonderfully, the sales associate had samples. I took a little piece of bittersweet almond bark. I thought about asking for more, but I didn't want to push it and my timer was ticking. Hell yes, it was good chocolate. Very good.

Before leaving, I bought something I could share: a 1 lb bag of milk chocolate nonpareils.

0–4 min / The Walk: Step out of the office and head west toward the Shops at Hudson Yards. This is the part where you breathe and anticipate.

4–9 min / The Selection: Enter the Shops and take the escalator to Level 4. Li-Lac's Hudson Yards outpost carries the full range - but if you want a place to start, the Nonpareils (milk chocolate discs blanketed in rainbow sprinkles, a New York classic) and the Almond Bark (freshly roasted almonds, chocolate, nothing else) are both exactly what a 15-minute break deserves. Everything is made in small batches using recipes that probably predate your grandparents. That's the 1923 spirit.

9–15 min / The Return: Walk back through the plaza. Don't rush it. The whole point is the fresh air as much as the chocolate - one is better with the other anyway.

Stepping away from focused work gives the brain a chance to shift into a more diffuse mode of thinking, where connections form more freely and problems that felt stuck start to loosen. You come back with more mental clarity and, counterintuitively, more capacity — not less. You could also come back with chocolate.

Break is over. Back to work. Share the chocolate.

item.title: Begin with Care
item.description: The first thing to understand about a small, tired oven is that it does not want to be improved. It has lived its life already. It is not interested in your goals.
item.content:encoded:
The first thing to understand about a small, tired oven is that it doesn't want to be improved. It has lived its life already. Seen tenants come and go. Seen cakes rise and fall, pans abandoned in the sink and found again with mild regret. It is not interested in your goals.

In a railroad apartment in Brooklyn, the oven sits where it has always sat, wedged between a narrow counter and a wall that remembers other colors. Two of the burners don't work. This is not a tragedy. It's simply a fact, like gravity, or the tendency of sugar to clump when humidity is high. You learn to work around it. You shift pots. You continue.

The oven itself does work. It works the way an old truck works: with sincerity, and on its own terms. It can reach 350 degrees. It can also reach 500 when you haven't asked it to. It takes its time warming up, and then, without announcement, it leaps. You learn that patience and vigilance are not opposites. They are the same practice in different clothes.

Many recipes call for 350. This is a kind of faith. It assumes an oven that behaves like a promise kept. Yours is more like a story retold: recognizable, faithful to the spirit, but with its own variations that arrive without explanation.

So you begin at 325.

Sometimes 325 is 350. This is a good day. The batter rises, the edges set, the center holds. A quiet satisfaction, the kind that doesn't need to be said.

Sometimes 325 is 300. The cake waits. Lingers in a long, slow becoming. You adjust the dial gently, the way you might speak to someone who startles easily. You don't demand heat. You invite it.

Sometimes 350 is 450. These are swift lessons. The top browns before the center is ready. You open the door and lay a small piece of foil over the pan, a gesture like covering someone with a blanket they didn't know they needed. You stay close. You watch. There is something in this watching that is not worry.

And then there is 400. For reasons that remain entirely mysterious, 400 is usually 400. You accept this without needing to understand it. Frozen pizza arrives with modest expectations and leaves with quiet success. It is enough.

At some point, you acquire a thermometer. It hangs from the rack like a humble witness. It doesn't judge the oven. It doesn't try to fix it. It simply reports what's true.

It shows you that what you believed was 350 has often been something else entirely. It asks you to look rather than assume. In this way, it's genuinely kind: it gives you not the answer you wanted, but the one that's actually useful.

The thermometer doesn't make the oven better. It makes you more aware. This is the more reliable improvement, and it lasts longer.

You begin to bake not by the number on the dial but by what the oven is actually doing on this morning, in this kitchen. You arrive at the counter without hurrying. You notice how long it takes to warm on a cold day. The smell when it's climbed too high. The way a cake pulls gently from the sides of the pan when it's truly ready, independent of what the timer says.

You still read recipes. You respect them. But you no longer receive them as commands. You translate them, quietly, into the language of your particular kitchen. Bake at 350 for 30 minutes becomes begin with care, watch closely, and respond to what you find.

Even if one day you move to a place with a new oven, level and responsive and well-behaved, you'll carry this. You'll preheat and then check. You'll open the door just to see. The thermometer comes along. It has earned its place.

This is not anxiety. It is attention. The old oven has helped you learn the difference.

It has made you patient. Humble before flour and sugar and heat and time. It has given you something a perfect appliance can't easily offer: the understanding that baking is not a transaction. It is a conversation.

Sometimes the oven answers clearly.

Sometimes it doesn't.

Either way, you continue.

item.title: Icebox Fruitcake
item.description: One of my earliest memories of baking is how I hated baking. Although that's not exactly right, I guess. I hated the thing that kept getting baked and pushed in front of me: fruitcake.
item.content:encoded:
One of my earliest memories of baking is how I hated baking. Although that's not exactly right, I guess. I hated the thing that kept getting baked and pushed in front of me: fruitcake. Ugh. The smell. The look. The texture. The taste. I still can't stand fruitcake. I'll grant that I haven't tried it in years, but something about it... some weird, candied fruit is ALWAYS in a fruitcake. I can't put my finger on it. I like everything that people typically put in a fruitcake, but when you put the ingredients together and put in to bake, what comes out is godawful. Oh, a big caveat - I don't like raisins. Maybe that's the thing. Maybe the raisins all melt out in the oven and then gel everything together to make one big sticky raisin log. Wait, is that how a fruitcake works? Is that the appeal? I really don't understand that. I understand Stuckey's peanut “logs” if you’re going for trunk shaped desserts. (If you don't know what they are, go on a cross-country road trip and stop at a Stuckey's. Brilliant.) But a raisin log with weird other "fruit" tastes is not cool.

My grandma was a good-hearted woman. So, she baked the gel raisin log for the lowbrow members of the family, but she also made a concoction called an "icebox fruitcake” for just me and her. In one way maybe she could've been trying take the sting out of the word "fruitcake" itself, to ease me into the word - like maybe I'd come to like the "real" ones if I didn't have a negative reaction to their name. But I don't think that's the case. I think she secretly hated the conventional, terrible version, too, and wanted a reason to make the icebox ones. Maybe she was a shade of iconoclast, too, in an oh so gentle, subversive Southern way. Going against tradition, fighting the powers, making icebox fruitcake. Our secret anti-establishment complicity. Man, I loved my grandma.

If you've never had it or never made it, you must. The "icebox" part means you don't have to bake it. You just mix everything together, put it in a loaf pan (best presentation), and put it in the refrigerator to cool. È squisito.

What do you need?

Graham Crackers — Never saw anything in the house besides Honey Maid. Didn't know there were even other brands. Crush them in a ziplock bag with a rolling pin or iron or whatever heavy you've got. Be careful not to burst the bag.

Chopped Pecans — I grew up in the south, so pecans were easy to find. NYC? They might be super expensive. Use walnuts if you can't find pecans. Some folks swear by almonds. I will swear at them. My grandma would have, too. This is not an almond dish.

Maraschino Cherries — Love these. You get to use a whole jar. Maybe this is why kid me liked this so much. When shopping for this recipe, buy two jars. Snack on one while you prepare the icebox fruitcake so you don't eat the ones that are supposed to go in the dessert.

Mini Marshmallows — Maybe little me liked this even more than the maraschino cherries. These are super essential.

Shredded Sweetened Coconut — You don't like coconut? Okay. Don't know what to tell you. No substitute. Go home.

Sweetened Condensed Milk — I always remember that little Carnation can. Never knew what else it was used for till I was an adult. My grandma didn't know about boiling the can itself to make Dulce de Leche, but I know she would've liked it. If you haven't done it, it's something you have to try. And Tres Leches. And Key Lime Pie. Also, a must in the Vietnamese iced coffee - a new shop just opened a block or so from me.

Raisins — Some recipes call for raisins. Raisins have already been discussed.

What do you do with all that?

Lightly spray two loaf pans with nonstick cooking spray. Crush the graham crackers using a food processor or add them to a large ziptop bag and crush using a rolling pin. Coarsely chop the cherries.

Combine the crushed graham crackers, pecans, cherries, coconut, marshmallows, and sweetened condensed milk in a large bowl and mix well. Add reserved cherry juice by the tablespoonful until the mixture comes together but isn't too soft. Between 2 and 3 tablespoons.

Turn out into the prepared pans and press flat with your hands. Cover and chill at least 6 hours, then cut into bars. Keep refrigerated.

Thank you, grandma, for the icebox fruitcake. I kind of always thought it was baked until I looked it up later in life. All good. Era di altissima qualità. So was she.

Here's the recipe.

item.title: Blind Baking
item.description: I bake when I am sad. It's hard to bake when you're frustrated. So I stay sad instead. Sadness brings cakes.
item.content:encoded:
I bake when I am sad. It's hard to bake when you're frustrated. So I stay sad instead. Sadness brings cakes.

When I feel like crying I go the refrigerator and pull out a couple of eggs and the butter. Room temperature eggs whip better. You only get 50-60% volume with cold eggs. You want a fluffy cake. Usually. And how can you cream hard butter with the sugar? There are tricks to get the eggs up to temp, but I haven't found a good one to get butter to the consistency I really want. There's the whole microwave burst thing, but some of the butter always melts a bit. It's close. But not the best. So I sit with my sadness at room temperature.

I pull out the correct measuring spoons for the various ingredients. I sort them in step order. 1 tsp. 1 tsp. 1 tbsp. 1/2 tsp. 1 tbsp.

I pull out the mixing bowl. I get the scale. Put a bowl on it. Tare. Add the flour. I rarely use the right measuring cups anymore. One leveled cup of flour never equals 124 mg of flour. Sometimes I just use a big spoon to scoop whatever and let the scale scale.

I use four lemons for three tablespoons of zest. It feels weird just using the lemons for their outer layer and then throwing the rest away. I typically put the naked lemons in ziplock bags and put them in the refrigerator, but then I forget about them and then just throw them away a month later instead. The kitchen smells like something is about to get better.

I cream the butter and sugar and zest together. Three to five minutes on medium in my Cuisinart stand mixer. People rave about Kitchen Aid. Ooh, they last forever! they say. Nope. I'm a Cuisinart person. They've always done me right. The creaming process works - yellow and dense to something pale and soft and almost hopeful looking.

I add the eggs one at a time. I crack each one into a separate little Pyrex first. Then I tip the little bowl into the mixing bowl, the machine running on medium-low. I don't want my fingers to get caught in the mixer, but this is the step. Always follow the steps. I watch the raw egg as it breaks apart and twirls into the buttersugarzest.

The sour cream goes in with the lemon juice. It looks reluctant to mix for a second but then it comes together.

I fold in the flour in three parts. Low speed. You don't want to overwork it. God, I am not gluten-free, therefore, I will allow gluten to bind this stuff together.

It bakes for 55 minutes. That's a long time for a cake, but maybe I guess not. Normal, I guess. I stand in the kitchen. I stand by the stove. I walk to the sink. I stand by the sink. Back and forth. I'm still sad and I don't want to sit down. I wash the dirty dishes. I stand.

The syrup is lemon juice and sugar cooked down until the sugar dissolves. I make it just before taking out the cake. Then I brush it on while the cake is still warm. It soaks in and the top goes a little tacky and dark and perfect. I do the sides too. Then I do it again. The recipe says a third at first and the rest after. I follow the recipe exactly.

The glaze is just powdered sugar and lemon juice whisked until it moves like not concrete and not water. Somewhere in-between. Maybe like lava? Kinda concrete-y, but seems smooth. I pour it over when the cake is cool.

Lemon pound cakes are for sharing. For company, you know? But I don't have anyone to share it with.

I don't even eat any of it. I just let it sit there. Maybe I'll have a piece in a couple of days.

I'm so sad I can't even see.

item.title: What we do at this hour
item.description: At 4 a.m., the kitchen is a small universe. The chaos of the world is suspended, and I, too, am suspended within it.
item.content:encoded:
The world is asleep, and so I move quietly through it, one cookie at a time.

At 4 a.m., the kitchen is a small universe. The lights are dim enough to see, not enough to awaken the sleepers. Every movement is deliberate, even when I am too tired to be deliberate. The spoon scrapes gently. The cabinet opens with a whisper. The oven door closes like a secret. The chaos of the world is suspended, and I, too, am suspended within it.

Except for the dog. There is always a dog. Should always be a dog.

Dogs understand the universe better than anyone else. So, in my case, it's Scrubber who understands it better than me. He sits beside me, still, alert, perhaps judging my kneading technique. There is no need for words. Sometimes he sighs. Sometimes he leans just a little, as if to say: I am here, and this is what we do at this hour. His presence is the quiet anchor of my meditation, and my sole audience.

I listen to music with one headphone, leaving the other ear open for the subtle sounds of the kitchen and the sighs of the dog. Sometimes I hum quietly - to him, to the dough, or to the cooling cookies - and the dough seems to respond with a pliancy it would not otherwise show. Perhaps it is listening. Perhaps it is indifferent. Either way, it folds itself gently beneath my hands.

While the cookies bake, I clean. Bowls, counters, trays. The work is simple, and yet necessary. A clean kitchen is a clean mind. And a dozen cookies, arranged in imperfect rows on the cooling rack, is a small triumph over impermanence. Even a monk would nod.

By 6 a.m., there is stillness. The cookies are warm. My dog is still beside me, contemplating the mysteries of butter and sugar. The house sleeps. The world sleeps. And I have done something - quietly, humbly, and without ceremony - that is entirely my own.

It is Zen. It is absurd. It is baking.

And if anyone were to wake up and ask what I am doing, I would simply smile, point to the tray, and say: Practicing impermanence, with chocolate chips.

item.title: The Mindfulness of Buttermilk-Complete Pancake Mix
item.description: There is something grounding about the simplicity: the soft thwump of powder hitting the bowl, the quick whirl of water folding itself into the mix, the smooth, quiet pour onto a preheated pan. It's the culinary equivalent of drawing a deep breath. Gentle, rhythmic, uncomplicated.
item.content:encoded:
There are days when I will happily whisk egg whites into stiff peaks, temper melted butter into warm milk, and fold batter like I'm handling diplomatic treaties. But there are also days when I reach unapologetically for the all-in-one buttermilk pancake mix. Add water, stir, pour, done. The purist in me winces; the human in me exhales.

Using a mix feels, in theory, like cheating. But in practice? It becomes its own kind of mindfulness. There is something grounding about the simplicity: the soft thwump of powder hitting the bowl, the quick whirl of water folding itself into the mix, the smooth, quiet pour onto a preheated pan. It's the culinary equivalent of drawing a deep breath. Gentle, rhythmic, uncomplicated.

In these moments, you realize that ease can be its own ritual. Not every act of baking needs to strive toward mastery. Sometimes the wisdom lies in removing complexity rather than adding it. Sometimes the most meaningful kitchen meditation begins with a box of Bisquick Complete and the humility to say, This is enough.

Lao-Tzu pondered the complete pancake mix:

When the bowl is simple, the heart becomes spacious.
When sweetness arrives without effort, joy needs no ornament.

Sometimes, a box mix collapses the distance between intention and outcome. There is no fear of overmixing, no rationing of buttermilk, no internal debate about griddle temperature. You breathe, you stir, you pour, and pancakes appear - small edible affirmations that life can be kind.

From this simplicity, unexpected clarity emerges. You pay attention to the small things: the first tiny bubbles forming on the batter's surface, the faint change in color around the edges, the gentle glide of the spatula as you flip. Each movement becomes a cue to return to yourself, to the steady rhythm of a morning not yet cluttered with responsibilities.

And there's joy - real joy - in watching these pancakes come together with almost laughable ease, especially when sharing them with family. The mix becomes less about shortcuts and more about accessibility: a chance for connection without the barrier of complexity. A reminder that pleasure does not always require labor, that memories can be made even when the batter comes pre-measured.

In the end, the zen of the box mix is simple: let go. Let go of the impulse to perfect, to impress, to justify. Let the ease be the ritual. Let the sweetness arrive effortlessly. And let the pancakes be enough as long as they're humble, fluffy, and warm.

item.title: Chomp Chomp’s Compendium of Forgotten Cookies - Introduction & Colophon
item.description: A surprisingly avid baker, Slavoj Žižek offers an introduction and colophon to this new cookbook that insist, correctly, that every recipe is a tiny ideological ball of dough waiting to be kneaded, folded, and exposed.
item.content:encoded:
I am extremely proud to present: Chomp Chomp’s Compendium of Forgotten Cookies - Thirty Four Confections of Desire, Discipline, and Semiotic Mischief With Full Metric Conversions. The final print publication date hasn’t been set, but it should be coming out sometime this Fall. Please email me for pre-ordering details!

Yes, while there are thirty-four recipes inside, this book is not merely a “cookbook.” It’s a mystery. A history. A Gothic tale. A farce. A philosophical tome. Indeed, the book’s Introduction and Colophon were written by Slovenian philosopher, Slavoj Žižek. I spoke with him about the project in the early stages, hoping to get a promise for a blurb on the back. Enthusiastic about my vision for the book, Slavoj asked if he could contribute something more substantial to the book, itself. He totally immersed himself in the history, the lore, and the cookies with the same intensity he brings to Hegel and Hitchcock. A surprisingly avid baker, Slavoj offers an introduction and colophon that insist, correctly, that every recipe is a tiny ideological ball of dough waiting to be kneaded, folded, and exposed.

So, in honor of getting our galleys from the printer and to drum up even more interest in the book, I’ve pasted those sections of the book below, in full. For more book stuff, you can also check out the recipes from the book in the Chomp Chomp recipes collection using the “Forgotten Cookies” category filter.

Chomp Chomp’s Compendium of Forgotten Cookies - Thirty Four Confections of Desire, Discipline, and Semiotic Mischief With Full Metric Conversions

A Revival for the Modern Baker

Every culinary tradition carries within it a concealed metaphysics. The small baked sweet on a kitchen table appears innocent, yet it expresses a culture's most anxious negotiations with desire, form, and meaning. Americans say cookie. Britons say biscuit. This naming divide is not trivial. It is the site where two societies decided, without ever admitting it, what sweetness should symbolize. The pastries collected here belong to the centuries before this decision hardened into habit. They emerge from a world where the rules of naming were porous, where a baked good could drift between identities like a traveler between inns. At the center of this drifting stands Hildevart Crumb, a figure who wanders through culinary history not as a stable presence but as a disruption, a trickster baker whose experiments unsettled every structure they encountered.

INTRODUCTION

To understand the cookie-biscuit divide, one must first accept that food is never only food. It is ideology in miniature. The American cookie descends from koekje and embodies softness, yielding textures, the pleasure of collapse. The British biscuit inherits the logic of twice cooked and embodies hardness, endurance, the moral suspicion that softness leads to ruin. These two pastries represent not competing recipes but competing fantasies of how pleasure should behave. A cookie promises surrender. A biscuit promises survival. Each becomes a cultural theory disguised as a snack.

Yet these theories did not arise organically. Before the divide, naming itself was unstable and unpredictable. A single pastry could be labeled biscuit, wafer, bread, or indulgence depending on where it was eaten and by whom. Market stalls, abbeys, and ships all produced their own provisional lexicons. The identity of a pastry was not fixed by its form but by the interpretive system that momentarily captured it. In this chaotic landscape Hildevart Crumb roamed like a catalyst for conceptual confusion. His pastries refused to stay still. They destabilized naming conventions wherever he went and revealed that the categories we now treat as natural were built on a foundation of accidents.

Crumb appears in scattered myths, half credible and half comic. He is said to have baked sweets so ambiguous in texture that entire markets erupted into argument over how to classify them. In London he sold his creations as biscuits to avoid the tax levied on luxury cakes. In Bruges he marketed the identical items as koekjes to charm a boat of Dutch traders. In a monastery he presented the same batch as devotional morsels to pacify a suspicious prior. And in each case the name stuck temporarily, as if the pastry absorbed the identity assigned to it in a moment of panic, improvisation, or mischief. Crumb did not simply rename pastries. He exposed the instability of the naming act itself.

In this sense Crumb becomes a proto-Chomp subject. He reveals the obscene underside of culinary ideology, the backstage machinery where cultures desperately attempt to impose meaning onto matter that refuses to cooperate. His baked goods were not failures of technique. They were eruptions of ambiguity that threatened to expose how arbitrary the cookie biscuit divide truly is. Crumb moves through history as the reminder that classification depends on repression. If his pastries had been allowed to proliferate, the neat binary would never have solidified. There would be no cookie as we know it, nor biscuit as the British insist it must be. There would only be the unresolved struggle between softness and hardness, expansion and restraint, indulgence and endurance.

A FINAL NOTE

The pastries in this collection vanished not because they were inferior but because they destabilized emerging norms. A sweet that was both crisp and soft at once presented too much conceptual danger. A treat that resisted classification threatened the entire symbolic order of the kitchen. Societies eliminated these ambiguous objects to preserve the illusion that their categories were natural. Yet the crumbs left behind reveal that culinary history is full of repression, misclassification, and anxiety. Even the most rigid biscuit inherits its existence from a long series of improvisations and contradictions that cultures have conveniently forgotten.

Reviving these pastries means reintroducing instability into a system that has tried very hard to forget it. Their unpredictable textures and contradictory behaviors expose the fragility of the categories we rely on. To bake them is to reenact the theoretical crisis they once provoked. Each irregular result is a reminder that the cookie biscuit divide is not destiny but the residue of a centuries long collective effort to stabilize meaning. The act of baking becomes an act of intellectual rebellion. It becomes a return to the moment when naming was still undecided and Crumb could interrupt the system simply by offering a tray of inconsistent sweets.

COLOPHON

This volume was assembled through a method that acknowledges the fragmentary nature of culinary history. Evidence appears in scattered forms. A monastic complaint about crumbs interfering with scriptural copying. A sailor's notation describing a ration that could double as a blunt object. A merchant ledger listing pastries whose exchange value fluctuated with humidity. A marginal note reputedly written by Crumb himself describing an experiment that caused a diplomatic misunderstanding after several pastries were mistaken for ritual offerings. These fragments do not reveal a coherent narrative. They reveal the ruptures through which history becomes intelligible.

The metric standards included here, identified as A1, B1, and F1, are not attempts to reconstruct authenticity. They serve as practical scaffolding for reenacting items that were originally produced under conditions where measurement was approximate and often irrelevant. Baking them today is not a nostalgic recreation but a theoretical exercise in confronting the instability that shaped their creation.

Crumb's legacy survived not through documentation but through the disturbances he left in the symbolic order of food. The disappearance of his pastries reflects the pressures that force culinary systems to suppress ambiguity. Yet their revival allows us to glimpse the moment before cookie and biscuit became rival national myths. In this sense these forgotten pastries allow us to taste the theoretical crisis that gave birth to the categories themselves. Each batch reopens the question that the system tried to close. What is a cookie. What is a biscuit. And what happens when a trickster baker like Hildevart Crumb refuses to let the answer stay fixed.

item.title: Flipmode Squad
item.description: Some of my earliest understandings of ritual came sizzling off a scuffed up frying pan on an electric coil range on Saturday mornings.
item.content:encoded:
Some of my earliest understandings of ritual came sizzling off a scuffed up frying pan on an electric coil range on Saturday mornings. While other families were going to football practice or scrubbing down the gutters or something, my dad and I were orchestrating our own liturgy: pancakes—silver dollars, specifically, each one no bigger than my palm. We weren’t chefs; we weren’t recreating some heirloom recipe from a distant grandmother. But we had something better: Parkay squeeze butter and Mrs. Butterworth’s syrup, those twin plastic totems of my childhood kitchen. Together they formed a sticky, fluorescent alchemy that felt like decadence, like permission, like childhood freedom itself.

Dad would pour the batter in neat spoonfuls, always careful, always methodical, and I would hover, waiting for the bubbles to appear so I could announce, with solemn authority, “Flipmode.” The sizzle that followed wasn’t just cooking; it was ceremony. When the pancakes were stacked into a little tower, steaming and soft, we would drench them until the plate resembled a shallow pool of amber syrup and glossy Parkay drifts. Decadent? Excessive? Absolutely. But this wasn’t about aesthetics. This was about Saturday, and Saturdays demanded indulgence.

What made these mornings especially magical was how superior they felt to the so-called “Men’s Pancake Breakfast” at our church. This was an event held every few months, supposedly a communal bonding experience. But the pancakes—God help those pancakes—emerged from the kitchen lukewarm, already defeated. They’d been sweating under sheets of aluminum foil, slowly transforming into soggy disks that resisted fork and joy alike. You’d pay ten bucks per person, a small tithe for mediocrity, with the promise that the money would go toward “new hymnals.” As if we didn’t already have hymnals stacked in every pew rack like neglected roommates.

I’d sit there, plastic fork in hand, thinking: Why am I eating cold pancakes in a church basement when I could be at home with Dad, drowning silver dollars in the good stuff? Even as a kid, I sensed the absurdity. Why finance the purchase of hymnals no one wanted to replace when I could be engaged in a far holier act - standing barefoot in my own kitchen, absorbing the warmth of the griddle, inhaling the buttery sweetness of Real Pancake Life?

At home, everything felt right. There was no pressure to socialize with people I didn’t know. No semi-burnt sausage links lined up like guilty offerings. No long folding tables draped in vinyl, sticky with decades of coffee spills. Just me, Dad, and a stack of pancakes engineered to an unapologetic, delicious excess.

Looking back, I realize those mornings weren’t just breakfasts. They were lessons in choosing authenticity over performance, warmth over obligation, home over the hollow promise of community events that misunderstood what community actually was. Pancakes were how we stitched Saturdays together. How we decided, silently but collectively, that joy was something you made for yourself: even if it came from a box, a bottle, and a squeeze-margarine container shaped for convenience.

And honestly? I’d choose those silver dollars over a hundred church breakfasts, hymnals or not.

item.title: Droopy
item.description: Yeah, you Droopy. You a sad dog.
item.content:encoded:
-You Droopy.

…

-Yeah, you Droopy. You a sad dog.

…

-Why you always look so sad?

-I don’t look sad. I’m not sad.

-You sad-looking. I’m namin you Droopy Dog.

Maybe he said it like: I’m namin you Droopy, dog. But I don’t think so.

I didn’t work much with Ant, but I’d come in for a day shift so I could have a weekend night off later that week. He typically came to the restaurant around 7 am to do prep and take in shipments. I was usually still up from getting off-shift around 2 or 3 am from the night before and keeping terrible waking hours, usually getting to sleep or passing out around 9 am or so.

He wasn’t a manager, so I thought of him as a sort of lieutenant at the restaurant. He pulled some of the admin work like signing for the shipments that managers didn’t always do and some of the kitchen scheduling. I was definitely a grunt in this restaurant’s army. But I wanted to keep it clear that I wasn’t his grunt. I wanted him to know that I was working hard and didn’t need any input or direction from him. Typically, if you look like you’re always rushing around and super busy, people don’t give you more shit to do. But I guess the serious and contemplative work-mode look I was trying to project just came out looking sad. Rushing seemed to be bumbling. Busy was doing something wrong. And to Ant, I always needed corrections.

I was prepping the fry station when he walked by and said

-You ain’t never spray that shit down.

pointing at the wall behind the grease bins.

…

-Why you ain’t spray that shit down?

…

-Droopy, get you some new spray and a rag from the dry and spray that shit down.

I’d sprayed that shit down the previous night until it gleamed. It was pristine. Stainless steel became platinum.

I drooped over to the dry without a word.

The dry was the walk-in pantry closet where we kept anything non-refrigerated. On the left wall were the cans and plastic tubs of secret, trademarked sauces and bags of flour and spice mixtures. On the back wall was a locked cage holding liquor bottles and mixers. On the upper portion of the right wall were cabinets housing napkins, printer paper, and other front of the house stuff. On the bottom were some unopened cleaning supplies and new rags, all stashed away from the food. I grabbed a bottle of concentrated all-purpose cleaner and a new rag.

The previous night there had been a nearly full bottle of concentrated cleaner already open in the mop and hose area, a recess at the back of the kitchen near the door leading to the dumpsters. It’d been opened only once before I’d prepared the last dilution to fill the spray bottle. This morning, though, Ant had poured both out.

Ant liked to run up the waste costs for the restaurant in different ways, mostly by writing off “spoiled” foods, but also more subtly (or absurdly?) by throwing out half of a slice of cheese for every whole one that he used or tossing every other slice of a cut onion. He checked off boxes of tomatoes as “not fresh.” Frozen meat: “freezer burn.” Bugs in the flour. Pouring out cleaning supplies. Whether it was his protest against low wages or whether he was just pathologically destructive, I don’t know.

I poured concentrate into the cleanest-looking spray bottle I could find all the way up to the drawn-on black line. The small 4 oz notch on the bottle wasn’t as concrete as the sharpie-drawn line, clicking a few ounces higher than the real notch. Ant always carried his black marker, forever checking and striking this and that. And as per his suggestion in a previous declaration on cleaning

-That notch don’t mean nothin. Anyways everybody use my line.

I filled the rest of the bottle with water from the dual-nozzled spigot in the mop nook, and took the new spray and new rag over to the fry station.

I half-heartedly sprayed a short burst of the all-purpose onto my shining grease backsplash wall and wiped it around. Ant came by while I was in mid-burst ahead of a second pass and said

-Boy you done good. Good. Put that down n come over here the sink. Let’s do the lettuce.

I started walking to bring the bottle to the mop nook before I was to wash the lettuce and Ant was to look on and not wash the lettuce but tell me everything I was doing wrong. He said

-Nah, don’t go back there. Put that there on your sink. Might need it later on.

…

-Or no, wait. You goin smoke? Let’s take a break.

I was following Ant to the back door when he stopped short and turned back

-You got a menthol? I only smoke menthols.

He had a pack of Newports in his back pocket.

-I’ve got Kools.

-Good man, Droopy. Good man. You got one for me, too.

(Not a question.)

I handed him one as he opened the door and pushed out with his other hand.

I sat down on a milk crate by a dumpster and lit my Kool with a disposable mini orange lighter that I’d named Chris’s Boat. I felt that I’d lose my lighters less often if they had names. Ant pulled out his pack of cigarettes where he had a lighter in the empty space from a few missing cigarettes. He noticed my glance and said

-I’m saving these for later.

We smoked in silence.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

item.title: On the Divergent Names of American Cookies and British Biscuits
item.description: The British–American split between “biscuit” and “cookie” is not simply a charming naming quirk but a kind of cultural symptom: each nation projects its own neurotic need for order or indulgence onto a fragile baked object, as if history itself were demanding a verdict on crispness versus softness.
item.content:encoded:
Anyone who has ever stood in a warm kitchen, late in the afternoon when the light begins to thin and the air settles into a kind of domestic stillness, has felt the small strangeness of language. A plate of sweet baked things sits on the table. In America, they are called cookies. In Britain, they are called biscuits. The objects themselves may resemble one another, but the names split away like two paths from the same door. The longer one looks at them, the more the difference between these names begins to feel deliberate, as if each had been shaped not only by history but by temperament. For centuries such small baked rounds drifted through kitchens, caravans, abbeys, and ports, shaped as much by scarcity as by taste, each era leaving a faint impression so that even the simplest sweet now carries the sediment of innumerable pasts.

The American word cookie is usually explained through the Dutch koekje. Dutch settlers carried the word to the colonies, and it took root in the New World with surprising ease. The official account stops there, neat and tasteful, but there is something in the sound of the word that suggests a deeper instinct. Cookie seems like a syllable every child invents when reaching for something warm and sweet. It rolls from the mouth with the soft impatience of desire. It feels older than its etymology, something shaped more by longing than by language. Even now the word seems to soften the room a little, as if it carried traces of soot from the earliest hearths that used it. Americans, for their part, have long spoken of cookies with an almost affectionate pride, claiming that a sweet ought to spread and settle into itself rather than hold rigidly to a predetermined form.

Across the Atlantic, biscuit carries the weight of history. It comes from the Latin bis coctus, or twice cooked, and it once referred to a hard, durable food for long journeys. British sailors spent months gnawing on these stoic wafers while the sea muttered beneath them. The modern British biscuit is gentler, but it still remembers its origins. It is crisp, tidy, self-contained, and able to withstand a brief baptism in hot tea without losing its dignity. The name speaks of endurance and habit, of something that has known hardship and become firmer for it. Britons sometimes speak of cookies with a faint, superior crispness, noting that a treat which slumps into softness cannot be relied upon during trying times.

Things become more tangled when one speaks across cultures. Say biscuit to an American, and you will conjure something else entirely, something soft and rising and almost tender. A biscuit on an American table is a warm, cloud-like bread that opens beneath a knife as if welcoming it home. It has nothing to do with its British cousin except the shared name that drifted into two meanings. This is one of those curious fractures that language collects over time, a reminder that words travel not only across borders but through households, affecting what they describe as they go. Americans, hearing the British speak of biscuits with such formality, often reply that a proper baked good should rise like ambition rather than sit obediently in a tin.

There are, of course, sensible explanations for these differences. Scholars trace migration, trade, and the slow drift of speech. Bakers adapt to local grains and ovens. Families alter recipes and pass them along until the changes harden into tradition. All of this is true, but it accounts only for the visible layers. Beneath them lie the stories people whisper to themselves about why something is called what it is, stories that cling to the edges of language as stubbornly as crumbs cling to cloth.

The less visible explanation is actually more sensible. According to a peculiar and little-known chronicle discovered inside a hollow wheel of parmesan in the storage of a long-abandoned monastery, an itinerant Flemish baker named Hildevart Crumb traveled through Europe in the early fifteenth century. He sold experimental pastries that were sometimes crisp, sometimes soft, and often unpredictable. In London he called them biscuits. A few weeks later, trying to avoid an angry merchant who accused him of selling counterfeit marzipan, he encountered Dutch traders and called the exact same pastries koekjes. The traders carried the word westward, and the people of the islands clung to the one they already knew. The story is unverifiable, yet it lingers with the strange logic of myth, the sort of tale that persists because it seems to fill a space that history left open.

Today the British continue to hold their biscuits with a sort of quiet discipline, each one a small exercise in order. Americans cling to cookies that spread, crack, and melt, each one a small act of unruly sweetness. In the end the difference is less about ingredients and more about the long, wandering life of words. Two nations inherited one craving and gave it two names. Both names stuck, and both continue to carry the flavor of the people who speak them, sometimes contentedly and sometimes with a quiet competitive satisfaction that neither side is willing to concede.

Timeline of the Cookie–Biscuit Naming Schism

1134
Cottage bakers in the Low Countries produce koeklings, which become popular among children and travelers.

1189
Monastic kitchens in England introduce Pilgrim’s Stoics, known for their durability and introspective effects.

1261
Hildevart Crumb attempts to unify pastry terminology at a regional fair, without success.

1327
Wayfarer’s Pucks appear in trade-route records as both food and defensive implements.

1410
The Biscuit Guild codifies rules for twice-baked goods. A brief rebellion follows among once-bakers.

1421
Crumb, evading a merchant dispute, alternates between biscuit and koekje when naming his pastries. Both terms proliferate separately.

1503
The Scribe’s Regret gains notoriety after several damaged manuscripts lead to new bakery restrictions in scriptoria.

1612
Koekje travels with Dutch settlers to the New World, gradually becoming cookie.

1769
British sailors critique American cookie softness. American bakers respond by developing variations with added richness.

1835
A failed international attempt to standardize terminology collapses during a multi-day dispute and several pastry-related accidents.

Present Day
Two traditions persist, each rooted in shared origins but culturally distinct.

—-

Glossary of Forgotten Cookie and Biscuit Names

Koekje
The Dutch term regarded as the seed of the American naming tradition, adopted by settlers and eventually naturalized.

Biscuit (Bis Coctus)
The twice-cooked original that defined shipboard sustenance and shaped the British sense of durability.

Experimental Pastries
Hildevart Crumb’s unpredictable creations that varied in texture, shape, and intention.

Twice-Baked Wafers
Hard travel provisions whose structure and temperament informed later terms.

Ship’s Stones
A common sailor’s name for early biscuits, sometimes used as improvised tools.

Traveler’s Flats
Flat, sturdy snacks suitable for journeys, often used as barter on rural roads.

Hearth Circles
Round, ash-dusted domestic bakes associated with household rituals.

Lord’s-Day Chewables
A category of Sunday-approved treats enjoyed quietly and sparingly.

Sweet Rounds for the Road
Pastries gifted to departing travelers, sometimes consumed prematurely.

Pilgrim’s Stoics
Notably firm biscuits that encouraged contemplative chewing and perseverance.

Twice-Browned Resentments
Bakes reheated out of frustration, developing a distinctively hardened exterior.

Mirthcakes
Sweets known to incite laughter or delight during village festivals.

Wayfarer’s Pucks
Portable, disc-shaped provisions that doubled as defensive projectiles.

Scribe’s Regret
A sweet with a propensity to drop crumbs on manuscripts, leading to smudged records.

Smalls of Uncertain Texture
Pastries difficult to classify, straddling the boundaries of multiple categories.

Oven-Wanderers
Mobile pastries said to shift on their trays during cooling, creating mystery.

Tidings
Edible tokens traditionally paired with news-bearing occasions.

Crustlets
Small, sturdy biscuits used to test the patience and temperament of children.

Mercantile Rounds
Market-stall offerings of inconsistent recipe but consistent presence.

Consolation Discs
Treats offered after disputes or disappointments, with mixed success.

Monk’s Embers
Ash-baked biscuits resembling hearth debris in both appearance and resilience.

Hildevart’s Folly-Cakes
Named in retrospect for Crumb’s failed attempt to standardize pastry terminology.

Dockside Cakels
Humidity-shaped pastries sold in portside stalls and docks.

Crumb Tokens
Edible stand-ins for small coins, exchanged during shortages.

Baker’s Lament
A soft, structurally unreliable cookie that struggled to hold its own shape.

Crumbwaifs
Small, fragile pastries known for disappearing unexpectedly from trays and shelves.

Koeklings
Offshoots or “children” of koekjes, often formed unintentionally from dough remnants.

Pan-Rounds of Reason
Pastries documented in monastic notes as “circles that defy logic.”

Misnomer Cakes
Pastries given names that never matched their form or flavor.

Folly Bisques
Attempts to moisten biscuits that resulted in ambiguous foodstuffs.

Crust-of-Argument
Shared between neighbors or family members after disputes.

Unnamables
Pastries left deliberately without names to avoid classification issues.

Softlings
Short-lived category of sweets abandoned for impractical softness.

Oath-Breakers
Infamously hard biscuits associated with expressions of exasperation.

Ash-Baked Flats
Early hearth-baked cakes cooked in or near embers, brushed clean before serving.

item.title: King Cake
item.description: I figured I could make a king cake. I figured I should make a king cake. Being from Mobile, Ala., the home of the first Mardi Gras celebration in America (not New Orleans, Mobilians are sensitive about that), I thought it'd only be right that I tried once, at least.
item.content:encoded:
"There's this little store down the road that sure makes a good king cake. I can just go to Walmart and get a pretty good one actually, but the one down there is pretty premium. If you were down here I'd show you. Tastes good. They've been doing them for a long time. Pretty well known. Famous for king cakes. Not far from where I live. They're pretty big. Better than Walmart I think. Though Walmart is pretty good. I just got one from Walmart this weekend. Saturday maybe. I had to go over there to pick up some things. I was walking through the produce section, and I saw the king cakes and put one in the cart. Their produce section is pretty good. And so is their bakery for some stuff. I guess only some stuff for their produce, though; I like their tomatoes. Their lettuce is horrible. It's hard to get a good tomato at a grocery store. You know that place down the road, can't think of the name, with the king cakes: they have good tomatoes when they're in season. Local produce. Mostly soybeans around here, but some good tomatoes, too. I was going to grow some tomatoes last year; I did some a couple of years ago. Came out with some good green ones we had on wheat bread with mayonnaise and salt and pepper for good tomato sandwiches. Never do the fried green tomatoes, but I've had some good ones. Man, you know? Those king cakes are good."

"Where are you now?" I asked my dad.

"Oh I was at home when you called. I'm in the car now going to get a king cake and see if that store down the road has any good produce. I'll text you the name of the store later if I can remember."

People were staring at the plastic cake carrier on the subway as I was bringing in my king cake to work. The carrier is see-through, so everyone could see the cakes with their gold, purple, and green sugar-sprinkled frosting. I'd like to imagine that they were covetous of the cake, wishing they could have a bite, but they were probably just annoyed. You're taking up too much room, get out of the way. Maybe I should've taken a Lyft.

I figured I could make a king cake. I figured I should make a king cake. Being from Mobile, Ala., the home of the first Mardi Gras celebration in America (not New Orleans, Mobilians are sensitive about that), I thought it'd only be right that I tried once, at least. Maybe it'd be on par with a local Louisiana bakery? The bar was high according to my father. At least better than Wal-Mart. But at the very least it'd be homemade by me and there are points for that, and I could always blame a screw-up on the recipe. I'd bring it in to work, because what did I need with a bunch of king cake at home. Also, I'd be crowned the office authority on king cakes.

Indeed, an authoritative primer for coworkers:

A King cake is a seasonal cake tied to Epiphany (January 6) and Mardi Gras, taking its name from the biblical Magi. In the U.S. Gulf Coast, the tradition dates to Basque settlers in 1718 and is now closely associated with Carnival season — celebrated from Mobile, Ala., home of America's first Mardi Gras, across to East Texas. The classic Louisiana version is a ring of cinnamon roll-style dough decorated in Mardi Gras colors — purple (justice), green (faith), and gold (power). A small plastic baby is hidden inside; whoever finds it gets good luck and the obligation to buy next year's cake.

I didn't have a recipe for one, so I went online and just searched "king cake recipe." Twenty million hits. I started sifting through the first hundred or so (seriously). I began eliminating many of them pretty quickly. Too pretentious. Too complicated. Too fancy. Needs a Kitchen Aid stand mixer (no, I'm a Cuisinart guy).

It came down to three recipes, one from a "Louisiana baker," one from allrecipes.com, and one from Epicurious. Epicurious used the most butter and didn't include any bastardization (Cream cheese? Really?), so I went with that one.

When I finally got around to making the cake, it was late on a Sunday night. I fell asleep before I could finish the frosting and had to wake up at 5am to get everything done before work. So I frosted it, sprinkled it, babied it, boxed it up, and took the subway.

But before I put the king cake out at the office, I had to make a warning sign about the plastic babies in the cakes. King cakes aren't a thing in NYC. It's not like everybody would know that they could choke on something inside of a braided cinnamon cake.

The warning in verse:

Please note
There is a plastic baby
In this Mardi Gras king cake.
It symbolizes good
Luck! Be careful
Not to bite into it.
Let me know if you get
The baby

Laissez les bon temps rouler!

After trying some cake, my coworker asked me, "So, you sent one of these to your father, right?"

"Maybe next year," I said. "You think he would like it?"

She is a pretty serious baker, taking her cakes to competitions around the country. She takes a week off from work every year to go to baking conferences. I hold her opinion in very high regard.

"I like it. You did good," she said. "He will love it. You're his son. He should know what his son can do. His opinion matters more than mine, but I think you got it perfectly."

I texted him a photo of my finished cake to let him know that, even outside of the South, I could indeed have some king cake for Mardi Gras.

"Looks good."

Then:

"Walmart king cakes not too good, though. They have some specialty bakers that do a real good job at Woods. It's the one here in Alexandria. Hope you have a great Mardi Gras."

Recipe here on chom.ps: King Cake
